ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Lorraine Hansberry — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two months of epigastric and back pain, weight loss, black stools and near-fainting in a woman of 32: examination, blood tests, and urgent upper endoscopy and pancreas-protocol CT

text.paragraph: Two months of epigastric and back pain, weight loss, black stools and near-fainting in a woman of 32: examination, blood tests, and urgent upper endoscopy and pancreas-protocol CT [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Burning, boring pain under the breastbone and through to the back for about two months, worse after meals and at night; black stools on and off for three weeks; two near-fainting spells; weight down 5 kg. [S]
An urgent care clinic put the pain down to indigestion and stress five weeks ago; she does not want it put down to stress again, and wants the cause found and told to her plainly, whatever it is. [S]
She wants to finish her play and to keep writing through whatever treatment she needs, with a clear head. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Lorraine Vivian Hansberry was born in Chicago on May 19, 1930, the youngest of four children of Carl Augustus Hansberry, a successful real estate broker who founded one of the city's first Black banks, and Nannie Louise (Perry) Hansberry, a schoolteacher. Her grandfather had been born enslaved. [D]

In 1937 her family moved into a house in the all-white Washington Park subdivision of Woodlawn in defiance of a racially restrictive covenant. The resulting case, Hansberry v. Lee, was decided in the family's favor by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1940. [D]
Her father died suddenly in Mexico in 1946 of a cerebral hemorrhage while planning to move the family there. [D]

She enrolled at the University of Wisconsin in 1948, left in 1950 for New York, and wrote for the newspaper Freedom. In June 1953 she married Robert Nemiroff. Sources differ on when they divorced (1962 or 1964); they continued to work together. [D]

A Raisin in the Sun opened at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre on Broadway on March 11, 1959, the first play by a Black woman to be produced on Broadway. It won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award; she was the first Black playwright and, at 29, the youngest American to win it. In 1962 she moved to Croton-on-Hudson, New York. [D]
One account dates the start of her illness to April 1963, when she began to suffer from fainting spells and attacks of nausea; tests pointed at first to what was suspected to be a duodenal ulcer. [D]

text.paragraph: 5 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Epigastric pain for about two months, boring through to the back and worse after meals and lying flat, with nausea, early fullness, a loss of 5 kg (8 percent of her weight), and pale, loose stools: an upper abdominal cause such as a bleeding ulcer or a pancreatic or duodenal tumor must be found. Upper endoscopy and pancreas-protocol CT booked this week
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to the documented collapse in pain and the account of a suspected duodenal ulcer. Superseded by the diagnosis at the second visit.
Iron deficiency anemia from chronic upper gastrointestinal blood loss: black stools on and off for three weeks, two near-fainting spells, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 ng/mL
S — Synthetic finding anchored to the documented account that she was told she had anemia and bleeding ulcers.

New hyperglycemia: A1c 6.6% and random glucose 132 mg/dL in a lean woman of 32 who is losing weight; new diabetes with weight loss can be the first sign of a pancreatic cancer, so it is to be confirmed and explained, not labeled type 2
S — Synthetic finding; superseded when diabetes due to the pancreatic cancer was recorded at the second visit.

Iron deficiency anemia from chronic upper gastrointestinal blood loss: black stools on and off for three weeks, two near-fainting spells, hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 ng/mL: active, confirmed [S]

New hyperglycemia: A1c 6.6% and random glucose 132 mg/dL in a lean woman of 32 who is losing weight; new diabetes with weight loss can be the first sign of a pancreatic cancer, so it is to be confirmed and explained, not labeled type 2: active, confirmed [S]

Medical oncology consultation within two weeks to review the endoscopy, CT and any biopsy with her and plan treatment if cancer is found. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma (2026); Khorana AA, et al. Potentially Curable Pancreatic Cancer: American Society of Clinical Oncology Clinical Practice Guideline. J Clin Oncol 2016;34(21):2541-2556 (PMID 27247221) (2016) [S]

Urgent work-up of epigastric pain with weight loss, anemia and new diabetes: upper endoscopy within days, pancreas-protocol CT of the abdomen with CT of the chest, blood count, ferritin, liver tests, lipase and A1c; pantoprazole until the endoscopy; return at once for fresh black stools, fainting or yellow eyes. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma (2026); Noel M, Fiscella K. Disparities in Pancreatic Cancer Treatment and Outcomes. Health Equity 2019;3(1):532-540 (PMID 31663065) (2019) [S]
Intravenous iron for iron deficiency anemia from blood loss, with a blood count at each visit. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma (2026) [S]

Distress and depression screening at each visit, plain explanations with written information, and support she chooses; she decides who is told and who receives each note. Guideline: Sanders JJ, et al. Palliative Care for Patients With Cancer: ASCO Guideline Update. J Clin Oncol 2024;42(19):2336-2357 (PMID 38748941) (2024); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]
